Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Deuteronomy 5, compiled from the sources I was able to access within usage limits.

## Deuteronomy 5 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1: "Then Moses summoned all Israel and said to them: Hear, O Israel, the statutes and ordinances that I declare in your hearing this day. Learn them and observe them carefully."

Moses opens his second and longest sermon in Deuteronomy by calling the entire nation to attention. The formula "Hear, O Israel" indicates that what follows is not incidental but essential for Israel's national survival (Jack Deere, cited at preceptaustin.org). The Pulpit Commentary notes that the "calling" refers not merely to the publicity of the address, but to "the clear voice which, breaking forth from the inmost heart of Moses, aimed at penetrating, as far as possible, to all" (Schroeder, cited in Pulpit). Ellicott adds that this verse makes clear that what follows is presented as "an actual exhortation, not merely a portion of a book." The Hebrew verbs form a fourfold pattern: hear, learn, be careful (guard/preserve), and do — all four are essential; hearing alone is insufficient (preceptaustin.org).

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/5.htm

### v. 2: "The LORD our God made a covenant with us at Horeb."

The covenant referenced is the Mosaic Covenant made at Mount Sinai (Horeb), not the Abrahamic Covenant (Pulpit, Constable). The phrase "made a covenant" is literally "cut a covenant" (*karath beriyth*), reflecting the ancient practice of sealing covenants through the cutting of a sacrificial victim (enduringword.com; preceptaustin.org). The LORD initiated this covenant — it was God's idea, not Israel's. Precept Austin notes that only Moses, Joshua, and Caleb of the original generation remained alive, yet Moses says "with us" because the covenant was with the nation as an organic whole, not merely with the individuals present at Sinai.

- URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-5-commentary
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-5.html

### v. 3: "He did not make this covenant with our fathers, but with all of us who are alive here today."

"Our fathers" refers to the patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob), with whom God made the unconditional Abrahamic Covenant, not the conditional Mosaic Covenant (Pulpit Commentary; preceptaustin.org). The Abrahamic Covenant unconditionally guaranteed Israel the Promised Land, but the Mosaic Covenant was given so they would *enjoy* the land — their enjoyment was contingent on obedience (preceptaustin.org). Ellicott explains the Hebrew idiom of contrast: "not only with our fathers…but with us also," meaning the covenant was intended for the present generation no less than for the first. Guzik (enduringword.com) emphasizes that Moses is making the covenant a present reality, not a historical relic: "It was a covenant of the living, not of the dead." Thompson is quoted: "The Horeb event was not simply an event of the past which concerned Israel's ancestors only, but was the concern of Israel in every age."

### v. 4: "The LORD spoke with you face to face out of the fire on the mountain."

"Face to face" is a figure of speech indicating direct, immediate communication without a mediator (Constable; Ellicott). It does not mean Israel saw a visible form of God — Deuteronomy 4:12 explicitly says "you saw no form; you only heard a voice" (enduringword.com). The phrase denotes remarkable transparency in communication. Both Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary note a slight Hebrew variation between the phrase used here (*b'panim*) and the one used for Moses (*el-panim* in Exodus 33:11), but the meaning is essentially the same: direct divine speech. God spoke to the people directly from the fire, just as He spoke to Moses, though Moses enjoyed closer communion.

### v. 5: "At that time I was standing between the LORD and you to declare to you the word of the LORD, because you were afraid of the fire and would not go up the mountain. And He said:"

Moses describes his mediatorial role. The Pulpit Commentary says, "I stood between the Lord and you; i.e., acted as mediator," and references the Septuagint (*heistēkein ana meson*) and Galatians 3:19, where the law is said to have been "ordained through angels by a mediator." Ellicott clarifies that the people's failure to go up the mountain was not merely due to fear but to God's express prohibition (Exodus 19). Keil & Delitzsch explain that Moses' mediatorial position was essential not so much at the proclamation of the Ten Words themselves, but "in connection with the conclusion of the covenant generally," which rendered the covenant possible given the people's terror at God's majesty (studylight.org). Enduringword.com notes that Israel could not bear such unhindered communication with God and therefore requested Moses to speak on their behalf.

### v. 6: "I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery."

This is the preface to the Decalogue, and Ellicott stresses that it is "an integral part of the Decalogue, and also the first part." Before any command is given, God declares who He is and what He has done. The pattern is grace before law: God redeems first, then calls for obedient response (Constable; enduringword.com). The Pulpit Commentary cites Schroeder: "The Law, the establishing rule for men, can proceed only from him who alone and over all stands fast; i.e., from God, specially as Jehovah." The declaration establishes that Yahweh is Israel's God by virtue of redemption from Egypt — His commands flow from His character and redemptive love, not arbitrary control (enduringword.com).

### v. 7: "You shall have no other gods before Me."

**Traditional Reading:** The first commandment asserts monotheism — there is but one God, Jehovah, and He alone is to be worshipped (Pulpit Commentary). "Before Me" is literally "upon My face" or "to My face" — meaning no other gods are to be brought into God's presence or sight (Ellicott; enduringword.com). Rashi is cited by Ellicott: "in any place where I am, that is, in the whole world." Guzik notes this does not mean other gods may be placed behind the true God; rather, Yahweh tolerates no rivals. Constable calls this "a call to respond to God's love by remaining faithful to Him instead of turning from Him to love something else more than Him."

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/5.htm
- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/5.htm
- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-5/

**Denominational Note — Commandment Numbering:** Protestant traditions differ on how to divide the Ten Commandments. The Reformed tradition counts v. 7 as the first commandment and vv. 8–10 as the second. The Lutheran and Roman Catholic traditions combine vv. 7–10 into a single first commandment and then split v. 21 (coveting) into two (the ninth and tenth) to maintain the total of ten (thegospelcoalition.org search result). The Gospel Coalition article notes it is "hard to choose between these alternatives," but the Reformed view "fits the text more easily." This means Catholic and Lutheran catechisms omit the explicit prohibition of images as a separate commandment, which historically led to the charge (noted by Clarke, cited at enduringword.com) that "to countenance its image worship, the Roman Catholic Church has left the whole of this second commandment out of the decalogue."

- URL: https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/deuteronomy/ (search excerpt)

### vv. 8–10: "You shall not make for yourself an idol … you shall not bow down to them or worship them; for I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on their children to the third and fourth generations of those who hate Me, but showing loving devotion to a thousand generations of those who love Me and keep My commandments."

**Traditional Reading:** The second commandment (in Reformed/Evangelical numbering) forbids the making of images for worship — both of false gods and of the true God. The Pulpit Commentary says it asserts "the spirituality of God" and prohibits "all deification of the powers of nature." Ellicott notes the Hebrew idiom closely connects verses 8–9: "Thou shalt not make to thyself any of these things for the purpose of bowing down to them or worshipping them." The commandment does not forbid artistic representation (God commanded images of cherubim, Exodus 25:18), but forbids images as aids to worship because "God is Spirit, and those who worship Him must worship in spirit and truth" (John 4:24; enduringword.com).

Regarding "visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children," both Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary emphasize the qualifying phrase "of those who hate Me" — the penalty extends only to those who continue in their fathers' hatred of God. Clarke is quoted: "This necessarily implies — IF the children walk in the steps of their fathers; for no man can be condemned by Divine justice for a crime of which he was never guilty" (enduringword.com). The focus is particularly on idolatry's national consequences across generations.

"Jealous God": Enduringword.com notes that "'zealous' might be a better translation in modern English, since 'jealousy' has acquired an exclusively bad meaning" (Cole, cited there). God's jealousy is His refusal to share His people's devotion with rivals.

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/5.htm
- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-5/

### v. 11: "You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not leave anyone unpunished who takes His name in vain."

**Traditional Reading:** "Take … in vain" is literally "lift up the Name of Jehovah thy God to vanity" (Ellicott; Pulpit). This forbids false swearing, profanity, frivolous use of God's name, and hypocrisy (claiming God's name while acting in ways that disgrace Him) (enduringword.com). Ellicott says, "Primarily, it is false swearing that is forbidden here; but the extension of the principle to vain and rash swearing, or the light use of the Name without real cause, is sufficiently obvious." The Pulpit Commentary adds that the prohibition also covers "all profanation of that Name by an irreverent or light use of it" (citing Leviticus 19:12). In the ancient Near East, sorcerers invoked deities' names for incantations; this command cut against that practice (enduringword.com, citing Thompson).

### vv. 12–15: The Fourth Commandment — the Sabbath

**Traditional Reading:** The Sabbath command in Deuteronomy differs from Exodus 20 in two notable ways: (1) it begins with "observe" (or "keep") rather than "remember," and (2) the reason given for Sabbath-keeping is the Exodus redemption rather than creation (Pulpit Commentary; Ellicott; enduringword.com). The Pulpit Commentary says the two reasons are "perfectly compatible; the one is fundamental and universally applicable, the other is subsidiary and special." The Exodus-based reason was fitting for a people about to enter the land, reminding them they were freed from slavery to be God's own possession.

The command includes rest for everyone — sons, daughters, servants, livestock, and foreigners — which Enduringword.com calls "a radical concept in the ancient world," declaring the essential humanity and dignity of all persons. The phrase "that your manservant and maidservant may rest as you do" (unique to Deuteronomy) emphasizes this humanitarian dimension.

Ellicott makes an intriguing typological observation: "If for the exodus of Israel we substitute here 'the exodus of Christ, which He accomplished at Jerusalem,' not so much by His death as by His resurrection, we have a reason for keeping not the Sabbath, but the Lord's Day."

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/5.htm
- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/5.htm
- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-5/

**Where Protestant Traditions Differ on the Sabbath:**

This is the most significant area of intra-Protestant disagreement in this chapter.

- **Reformed (Continental/Calvinistic) View:** John Calvin argued the specific day is a matter of indifference; what matters is the principle of regular rest and worship. The Heidelberg Catechism reflects this (learn.ligonier.org search result). The Sabbath is typological of spiritual rest in Christ, and the day of worship under the new covenant is largely a matter of Christian freedom.

- **Reformed (Puritan/Westminster) View:** The Westminster Confession of Faith (21.7) and the 1689 Baptist Confession (22.7) teach that the fourth commandment contains a "perpetual commandment, binding all men in all ages … [to keep] one day in seven for a Sabbath." The day has shifted from Saturday to Sunday (the Lord's Day) due to Christ's resurrection. This is often called the "Christian Sabbath" view. Recreation on Sunday was disputed between the Continental and Puritan views (Ligonier search result).

- **Baptist (MacArthur/Grace Community Church):** John MacArthur at gty.org classifies Seventh-Day Adventists and Seventh-Day Baptists as "strict sabbatarians" who keep Saturday. He also notes that "Christian sabbatarians" (many Puritans and Reformed) treat Sunday as a new Sabbath, but he questions whether this is correct. MacArthur represents the view that the Sabbath was a sign of the Mosaic Covenant specifically for Israel and is not binding on new covenant believers (from search excerpt).

- **Lutheran:** Lutherans follow a different Decalogue numbering (combining commandments 1–2 and splitting commandment 10). On Sabbath observance, the Lutheran tradition (see the search excerpt from TGC) generally holds that the Sabbath command was part of the ceremonial law fulfilled in Christ, and Christians are not bound to a specific day, though they freely gather on Sunday in honor of the resurrection.

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduringword.com/Guzik):** Guzik teaches that "under the new covenant, no one is under obligation to observe a Sabbath day (Colossians 2:16-17 and Galatians 4:9-11)." The Sabbath was "a shadow of things to come, but the substance is of Christ." Every day is a day of Sabbath rest in Christ's finished work. However, Guzik affirms the importance of a weekly day of rest for human well-being, and suggests Sunday is "more appropriate" because of the resurrection. He also stresses the command to work six days, quoting Clarke: "He who idles his time away in the six days is equally culpable in the sight of God as he who works on the seventh."

### v. 16: "Honor your father and your mother, as the LORD your God has commanded you, so that your days may be long and that it may go well with you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you."

**Traditional Reading:** The fifth commandment is the foundation of all social order — the family is the germ of society, and where parents are not honored, "a flaw lies at the basis, and the stability of the entire social fabric is endangered" (Pulpit Commentary). The Deuteronomy version adds "as the LORD your God has commanded you" and "that it may go well with you" — both absent from Exodus 20 (Pulpit; Ellicott). Ellicott notes that Paul cites this Deuteronomy form of the commandment in Ephesians 6:2–3. The command applies to children of all ages and includes prizing parents, caring for them, and showing respect (enduringword.com). Grant's Commentary (studylight.org) notes that this is "the first commandment with promise" (Ephesians 6:1–2) and that even harsh or irresponsible parents are to be honored.

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/5.htm
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/deuteronomy-5.html

### vv. 17–20: Murder, Adultery, Theft, False Witness

These four commandments are worded identically to Exodus 20 (Ellicott). The Pulpit Commentary notes a progression in the second table of the law: from outward deeds (murder, adultery, theft), to sins of speech (false witness), to sins of the heart (coveting). Grant's Commentary adds that the sixth commandment does not forbid all killing — Israel was commanded to kill Canaan's inhabitants and execute criminals; it forbids individuals taking life into their own hands (murder as distinct from manslaughter or just execution).

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/5.htm
- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/5.htm
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/deuteronomy-5.html

### v. 21: "You shall not covet your neighbor's wife. You shall not covet your neighbor's house or field, or his manservant or maidservant, or his ox or donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbor."

**Traditional Reading:** The tenth commandment is unique in addressing inward desire rather than outward action, revealing that sin begins in the heart (enduringword.com). The Deuteronomy version has several differences from Exodus 20: "field" is added (appropriate now that Israel is about to become a landowning people), the wife is placed first and separated from the property list, and two different Hebrew verbs are used — "desire" (*chamad*) for the wife and "covet" (*'awah*) for property (Pulpit Commentary; Ellicott). The Pulpit Commentary says the separation of the wife and the change of verb emphasizes her distinct status — she is not merely part of a man's property. The TGC commentary notes this is "in line with the strong sensitivity to women shown by Moses throughout the book" (search excerpt).

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/5.htm
- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/5.htm
- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-5/

**Denominational Note — Catholic/Lutheran Numbering:** As noted above, Roman Catholic and Lutheran traditions split this verse into two commandments: the ninth ("you shall not covet your neighbor's wife") and the tenth ("you shall not covet your neighbor's goods"). This allows them to combine vv. 7–10 into a single first commandment and still have ten total.

### v. 22: "The LORD spoke these commandments in a loud voice to your whole assembly out of the fire, the cloud, and the deep darkness on the mountain; He added nothing more. And He wrote them on two tablets of stone and gave them to me."

**Traditional Reading:** "He added no more" means God spoke only these Ten Words directly to the people; all further legislation came through Moses (Pulpit Commentary, citing Herxheimer; Ellicott). The Pulpit Commentary notes this phrase echoes Numbers 11:25 ("and they added not"), meaning the direct divine speech ceased after the Decalogue. "With a loud voice" underscores the public, unmistakable nature of the revelation. "Two tablets of stone" anticipates what is recorded historically in Deuteronomy 9:10–11. Constable notes that God's direct communication with the whole assembly marks the uniqueness of this revelation in Israel's history.

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/5.htm
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-5.html

### vv. 23–27: Israel's Fear and Request for a Mediator

When the people heard God's voice from the blazing mountain, the tribal heads and elders approached Moses. They acknowledged they had witnessed something unprecedented: "God speak with man, and man still live" (v. 24). Yet they feared further direct contact would kill them, so they asked Moses to serve as intermediary: "Go near and listen … we will listen and obey" (v. 27). Ellicott notes the speech of the elders is described more fully here than in Exodus 20. The Pulpit Commentary says the more detailed account is fitting for a direct address to the people rather than a historical narrative. Ellicott observes that "the instinctive dread of death awakened by the Divine presence … bears eloquent testimony to the truth that man was made to bear the Divine likeness, and to live a holy life."

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/5.htm
- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-5/

### vv. 28–29: God's Response

God approves the people's words: "They have done well in all that they have spoken" (v. 28). But then comes the poignant divine lament: "If only they had such a heart to fear Me and keep all My commandments always…" (v. 29). The Pulpit Commentary comments that "God approved of their words because they expressed a proper reverence … but knowing their fickleness, and proneness to forget and depart from him, he added, Oh that there were such an heart in them." Enduringword.com calls this "a sigh from the Divine heart that echoes Jesus' tears over Jerusalem." Constable says these words "reflect God's great love for Israel and His desire that His people experience His blessing."

Ellicott makes a striking connection: the promise of a prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:18–19) was given at this very moment. God acknowledged the people's need for a mediator like themselves by promising the ultimate Mediator. Ellicott writes: "He who gave the Law on Sinai died under it on Calvary, and provided for its observance for ever." The Hebrew phrase "Who will give that there shall be this heart in them?" (Ellicott's literal rendering) has its answer in the new covenant promise: "I will put my laws in their hearts" (Hebrews 8:10, cited by Ellicott).

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/5.htm
- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/5.htm
- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-5/
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-5.html

### vv. 30–31: "Return to your tents" / Moses Stands as Mediator

God tells the people to return to their tents (their camp dwellings) while Moses remains "here with Me" to receive the full body of commandments, statutes, and ordinances. This formally establishes Moses' ongoing mediatorial office. The Pulpit Commentary notes the contrast: the people go back to ordinary life, while Moses stays in the divine presence to receive the law he is to teach them. Ellicott ties this to the promise of the coming Prophet (Deuteronomy 18:18–19).

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/5.htm
- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/5.htm

### vv. 32–33: "So be careful to do … you are not to turn aside to the right or to the left. You must walk in all the ways that the LORD your God has commanded you…"

Moses concludes with an exhortation to careful obedience. "Not to turn aside to the right or to the left" is a recurring Deuteronomy phrase (cf. 17:11, 20; 28:14; Joshua 1:7) signifying exact, undeviating adherence to God's commands (Pulpit Commentary, citing Ainsworth). The Pulpit Commentary also cites Calvin: "To receive what God enjoins is only half obedience; it belongs thereto also that nothing be required beyond this. We must not desire to be more righteous than as we are taught by the Law." The promised result is life, prosperity, and prolonged days in the land — the blessings of covenant faithfulness (Constable). Precept Austin notes the chapter opens and closes (vv. 1, 32–33) with a charge to follow carefully the divine stipulations, forming an inclusio around the Decalogue.
